name: Maitreyi
summary: Maitreyi is a woman sage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. When Yajnavalkya offers her his wealth before leaving home, she asks only for the knowledge that leads to immortality.
about: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad presents Maitreyi as one of the two wives of the sage Yajnavalkya, along with Katyayani. The text says that when Yajnavalkya decided to leave household life, he offered to divide his property between them. Maitreyi asked whether wealth could make her immortal, and when he said no, she asked him to teach her what he knew. He then taught her that all that we love is dear for the sake of the Self. The Mahabharata and the Grihya Sutras describe a Maitreyi who never married, so scholars debate whether these are the same woman. Estimates place her around the 8th century BCE. Later commentators, including Shankara and Sureshvara, wrote on the dialogue.
kidSummary: Maitreyi was a wise woman of ancient Mithila. When her husband Yajnavalkya wanted to give her all his riches, she asked a special question: could money make her live forever? She chose wisdom over wealth, and her talk with him is still read today.

story.title: A husband's decision
story.text: Yajnavalkya tells his two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani, that he is ready to leave home and live as a seeker. He wants to share his belongings so both of them will be well looked after.

story.title: A big question
story.text: Maitreyi asks what would happen if the whole earth, filled with wealth, were hers. Would that make her live forever? Yajnavalkya answers that she would only live a comfortable life.

story.title: Choosing wisdom
story.text: Maitreyi decides that riches she cannot take beyond life are not what she wants. She asks Yajnavalkya to share the knowledge that brings freedom.

story.title: The dearness of the Self
story.text: Yajnavalkya teaches that we love people and things because of the Self within, and that knowing the Self is what matters most. He is pleased that she asked.

story.title: A seeker's road
story.text: Another tradition, found in the Mahabharata and the Grihya Sutras, remembers a Maitreyi who never married and lived as a lifelong ascetic and teacher.

teaches: Wisdom can matter more than wealth
Be curious about your own inner self

facts.text: Maitreyi asks whether she would become immortal if the whole earth, full of wealth, were hers. Yajnavalkya says no, so she asks him to teach her what he knows instead of dividing the property.

In the dialogue even the gods are said to be dear not for their own sake but because of the Self; scholars read this as saying every kind of love, from parents to the whole world, reflects love of the Self.
To show how the Self is reached, Yajnavalkya says a drum's sounds can only be grasped through the drum or the drummer, and the same goes for a conch and its blower, or a lute and its player.
A lump of salt dropped in water dissolves and cannot be picked out again, yet every sip tastes salty. Yajnavalkya uses this to show the Self is everywhere, like a boundless mass of knowing.
After hearing that there is no separate awareness after death, Maitreyi tells Yajnavalkya he has confused her, and he replies that he did not mean to, and that his teaching is enough to understand.
The commentator Sureshvara has Yajnavalkya say that in the story of Shiva and Uma, she took half of his body out of love, but Maitreyi wants to win the whole of him, the Self.
The Mahabharata describes a Sulabha Maitreyi who never marries and explains Advaita, the oneness of all, to King Janaka.
After Yajnavalkya leaves home and becomes a renunciant, Maitreyi is said to have taken up the wandering life of a renunciant herself.

In the second telling, Yajnavalkya describes the Self as 'not this, not this': it cannot be grasped, does not decay and is never harmed. He then tells Maitreyi she has the teaching and leaves to become a renunciant.
Before leaving, Yajnavalkya, having been a student, a householder and a forest dweller, wants to become a renunciant and offers to divide his property between Maitreyi and his other wife, Katyayani.
The Upanishad pairs her with Katyayani, who is described as having the practical knowledge of household matters, while Maitreyi is the one drawn to metaphysics.
In the four known versions of the story, Maitreyi challenges Yajnavalkya's account of the Self, and the commentator Sureshvara saw the exchange as profound on both sides.
Scholars read her differently: Wendy Doniger sees a story of a Brahmin with two wives, while Karen Pechilis sees a theologically minded woman who asks the right questions.
Shyam Ranganathan suggests Maitreyi turned down the money because, as a brahmavadini who may already have been a successful teacher, she had no need of it.

quiz.why: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad names Yajnavalkya as her husband.

quiz.q: What did Maitreyi ask Yajnavalkya about wealth?
options: If it could make her immortal
If it could buy a palace
If it could make Katyayani happy
quiz.why: She asked whether all the wealth of earth could give immortality.

quiz.q: Which objects does Yajnavalkya use to explain that a sound is grasped through its source?
options: A drum, a conch and a lute
A bell, a flag and a spear
A river, a tree and a hill
A bow, a horse and a chariot
quiz.why: The dialogue pairs each sound with its drum, shell or lute and the player.

quiz.q: What did Maitreyi choose instead of the property?
quiz.why: She asked Yajnavalkya to teach her what he knew.

quiz.q: Who was the other wife of Yajnavalkya?
quiz.why: Katyayani is named as his other wife in the Upanishad.
